Nothing seems to have any real design features; instead, the look feels as simple and muted as possible, with everything in matte. I think it's the overly simple styling and lack of flair or detail in anything. Now\u2026 I shouldn\u2019t be throwing stones in my own house. I know my home looks very dated, like stepping back into 2005. While I had high-end finishes (for the time) and nice furniture, I can\u2019t say it looks refreshed or great in 2025. I guess what I\u2019m trying to ask is\u2026 does anyone else feel the same way? Does anyone else look at design catalogs or trends and feel completely stuck in between? I want to replace my cherry cabinets and granite countertops, but I just can\u2019t get behind quartz or marble, and white or green cabinets. I seriously can't stand the look! other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "sah-upstate4", "author_name": "sah_upstate4 (zone 5b - NY)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/sah-upstate4", "date": "2025-03-06", "text": "\"What kind of damage are you talking about? Eaten leaves? Eaten branches? Bark stripped branches? Bitten branches? I'm personally not familiar with rabbit damage.\" I'm in a similar situation as @prairiemoon2 z6b MA: in winters like this one where we get relatively deep snow cover over an extended period, rabbits tend to change their diet to mostly woody material and they'll go after the lower limbs of any shrubs or trees they can reach, which is higher than normal when aided by snow or ice accumulation. Rabbit damage looks like \"clean\" pruning cuts, since their incisors are very sharp, as opposed as to the ragged/torn damage left by deer. On larger limbs (especially on apple trees), they'll strip the bark completely and can totally girdle (and likely kill) the trunks of younger plants I fence as many of the rabbit \"favorites\" as I can: Fothergilla, Hamamelis, Hydrangea quercifolia, Japanese maples, anything in the apple family. I also definitely protect any shrubs/trees that were newly planted in the fall, but I don't have the time or energy to fence everything, and if the snow persists for a while, they'll go after anything. The last few winters, with warmer temps and more minimal snow cover here in upsate NY have been a bit of a \"reprieve\", but this winter has been significantly more \"wintry\", and the rabbit feast has resumed. Just over the past few weeks, they've started chewing on my unfenced Clethra, Diervilla, Itea, and any lower limbs on nearly any unfenced young trees. The only option now is to be \"generous\" and frequent with Liquid Fence sprays for things they've already started on. I typically don't try to \"repair\" any of the damage they do, and just keep an eye on how the plant regrows in summer. If I'm not happy with how it looks, I'll make \"adjustments\" in the following dormant season.", "images": []}}

title: Almost Corned Beef Time! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "chloebud", "author_name": "chloebud", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/chloebud", "date": "2025-03-05", "text": "I got my corned beef yesterday for St. Paddy\u2019s Day.  It\u2019s one of my favorite meals, and I\u2019ve shared my version before.  How about yours? Corned Beef and Cabbage From The New Basics Cookbook; Serves 4-6 1 corned beef (5-6 pounds...I prefer a flat cut)2 onions, studded with 3 whole cloves (onions can be halved or quartered)4 carrots, peeled and halved2 ribs celery, halved4 sprigs Italian parsley 1 green cabbage (about 3 pounds), cut into 6 wedges (See *Note below)12 small red new potatoes6 small leeks (white part and 2 inches of green), well rinsed (See *Note below)6 carrots, peeled and cut into 2 1/2-inch lengthsSalt and fresh ground pepper, to taste4 T. chopped Italian parsley Place corned beef in large kettle or dutch oven. Add the onions, halved carrots, celery, and parsley sprigs (use seasoning packet if provided with your corned beef). Cover with cold water and bring to a boil. Reduce heat, cover, and simmer for 2 3/4 to 3 hours, turning beef over in broth every 30 minutes. DO NOT allow water to boil again; keeping at low simmer will ensure tenderness. When it is very tender, remove it from kettle and keep warm. Strain the broth and return it to the kettle. Add the cabbage, potatoes, leeks, cut-up carrots, salt and pepper, and 2 T. of the chopped parsley. Bring to a boil; reduce heat, cover, and simmer until vegetables are tender, 30 minutes. Arrange beef on warmed serving plater, and surround it with the cooked vegetables. Ladle broth over beef and vegetables, and sprinkle with remaining 2 T. chopped parsley. Optional - serve with Horseradish Cream Sauce (below). *Note: Keeping the core in the cabbage wedges will help hold them together while cooking. Remove the core before serving. After thoroughly washing, leeks can be tied together with kitchen twine/string; remove for serving. Horseradish Cream Sauce This makes 2 cups of sauce. The recipe can easily be halved, as needed. 3/4 cup whipping cream1/2 cup mayonnaise1/2 cup prepared horseradish, drained2 T. Dijon mustardPinch of sugarSalt and fresh ground pepper, to taste Whip cream in bowl until it forms soft peaks. Combine mayonnaise, horseradish, and mustard in another bowl. Fold in whipped cream. Add sugar, salt and pepper. Stir well, and transfer to serving bowl. ETA - Just wanted to add I got this recipe from the Silver Palate girls (New Basics Cookbook) long ago.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~278115867", "author_name": "beesneeds", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~278115867", "date": "2025-03-08", "text": "The tradition came when Irish immigrants encountered Jewish deli's in their new home, America. Their \"old country meat\" wasn't as available, but their neighbors had this awesome cheaper substitute called corned beef. A kind of reverse happened too- the Irish habit of pickled meat led to the popular New England boiled dinner. Corned beef and cabbage was still cheaper and more widely eaten at the time, and so got equated with everything Irish (or at least American Irish) on St. Patricks. They have a strange habit of growing sideways on the top of a stem (as a dinner plate dahlia would, instead of facing up).", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b1b2e21307c9ff69_1372-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/9972d54507c9ff69_1372-w500-h375-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2982fa4907c9ff6a_1372-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5bc2dd6707c9ff6a_1373-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "oldmoses", "author_name": "Moses, Pitt PA, cold W & hot-humid S, z6", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/oldmoses", "date": "2025-03-07", "text": "Jena, You commented that your roses' blooms are turning sideways as shown in your photos.  In your first photo, I see a not yet open bud turned sideways with what looks like a scar on the neck of the bud on the side where the bud is facing.  That could be rose midge fly damage done when the bud was younger, as young as when the bud was smaller than a pea. Are you aware of the rose midge fly and the considerable damage its maggots do to rose tip growth?  Destroying flower production at new growth points at the worst, and damaging flowers from blooms either opening improperly, or grossly deformed flowers, are signs of rose midge fly. Damage is mostly done at the very earliest stage of a flowering tip, or a little later on until the stage where the young bud is the size of a garden pea.  After reaching a pea size, rose buds, if not caught by RMF maggots, usually are not eaten being too tough, and go on to grow and bloom normally. Rose Midge Fly is a serious pest in the North East USA, having a particular stronghold in many localities.  Unfortunately, there are no dependable organic control methods I know of, so conventional insectIcides are sprayed on a strict schedule to control the damage done by RMF. title: Way early but why not?  Menu planning... | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "anniedeighnaugh", "author_name": "Annie Deighnaugh", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/anniedeighnaugh", "date": "2025-03-07", "text": "In late May, God willing and the creek don't rise, I will be having my girlfriends from college for an overnight.  Two will be staying...not sure what the 3rd with/without her husband will be doing.  So it may be 5 or 6 of us.  The couple has an RV so they may drive over and park it here while the other 2 will sleep in my guest room. Or if she comes without him, her daughter is nearby and she may stay with her instead and then return for breakfast.  Not really sure yet. The plan is to arrive in the afternoon for tea time...3-4 ish.  Stay for dinner, stay overnight and leave after breakfast the next day.  So essentially 2+ meals. Diet wise, no major restrictions though 2 are diabetic, but will eat regular food including sweets anyway within reason.  So not restricted, but I'd like to be mindful of it. Not sure what to do for tea time which may transition into appetizers before dinner with maybe wine and nonalcoholic drinks.  I suspect the dried apricots with mascarpone and walnuts will be involved though.  Probably Dolly Madison's Cinnamon tea cakes too which goes well with tea or wine.  Plus more fruit, nuts, veggies, dip, cheese and crackers and salami for transitioning to wine or other drinks. Dinner, I'm thinking crock pot so I don't have to tend anything while they're here.  So most likely my roast pork with orange and cranberry, or my crockpot ham.  Not sure of sides, though a tossed salad will be in the mix as will my homemade biscuits.  Or I could make my crockpot hungarian goulash with egg noodles.  I recently made us chicken breasts in the crock pot a la NYTimes that was really tasty and served with rice/grains from TJs on the side...still pondering veggie side dish depending on the entree.  There too I like a casserole that can be prepared ahead and just baked off before serving...or something simple like hericot vert and carrots that are blanched ahead of time and just tossed with olive oil and garlic to heat through before serving.  Also pondering dessert...maybe something easy but good like coffee ice cream with maple syrup and walnuts.  The creamery will be open and their ice cream in superb.  Or an Italian ricotta cheese cake?  Pound cake cubes topped with macerated fruits?  Or maybe the pound cake with ice cream and chocolate sauce?  Or make it easy and get the assorted cookies from the bakery...they are delish. Breakfasts are usually fairly easy as DH will help with eggs which we usually scramble with ham, onion, peppers and mushrooms. I'll have some fresh fruit and yogurt and bread/muffin options with coffee, tea and juices.  Most likely more individual as DH and I are early risers, but our overnighters are not. They will also bring stuff. Lots of time to nail it all down, but fun to ponder. What would your druthers be if you were coming?", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "theforgottenone1013", "author_name": "theforgottenone1013 (SE MI zone 5b/6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/theforgottenone1013", "date": "2025-03-09", "text": "The information in the link you provided mirrors the information in the link I gave as well as the statements I have made. Warmer soil temps speed germinaton for nearly all vegetables, with the optinimum soil temperature for most being at least 75 degrees. With many, even cool season plants, prefering temps above that.Also, there is no denying the fact that the longer a seed spends in cool, moist soil the higher the chance of that seed rotting or being attacked by fungus or disease. There is little to gain, and seed to loose, in planting seed in cool soils if they are just going to take 2 weeks or longer to germinate and then grow slowly once they do. main_question: {"author_id": "perennialfan275", "author_name": "perennialfan275", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/perennialfan275", "date": "2025-03-09", "text": "I'd like to start by saying I don't think we talk about other species (other than ourselves) enough here (not just on this site, but pretty much everywhere), so I'm trying to change that. I hope others here will assist me in this endeavor. Despite this troubling news, there is hope for these fragile and beautiful creatures. Planting some native plants (host and nectar plants), and reducing pesticide use can go a long way to helping them. https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cwyjkn729gpo", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mxk3", "author_name": "porkchop_z5b_MI", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mxk3", "date": "2025-03-09", "text": "This is not good.  It's not just the butterflies -- all insects are on the decline.  The problem is multifaceted, but something as simple as incorporating native (to your area) species of flowering annuals/perennials in your flower beds and native shrubs and trees can go a long way. I'm not a native purist -- I do think there is a place for both natives and non-natives in an attractive landscape.  Incorporating proportionately more natives into my property at this house was intentional, and I have noticed a greater diversity of insects who visit -- not just butterflies, but all pollinators.  Along with that, more birds.  Remember, birds feed their young insects - few insects = few birds.   It takes time, but that old saying holds true -- plant it and they will come. What's not attractive about oaks, maples, birches, or tuliptrees?  Those are all native to the midwest and beautiful trees.  For midwestern shrubs - fothergilla, winterberry hollies, some virburnum, and various types of conifers, to name a few.  Tons of different outstanding native perennials, wherever you happen to be located. ETA:  And STOP nuking the cr*p out of your plants and lawn.  When I see a perfectly manicured lawn, to me that is not beautiful it is sad -- devoid of diversity and not supporting the ecosystem in any way; in fact, destroying it by all the chemical application.  Not every spot on a plant need spraying with something (even organics can be very harmful), and no one driving down the street cares if you lawn has a patch of violets in it, it's all green so it's fine. title: Il problema degli elettrodomestici a incasso | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-338829274", "author_name": "Cuiprodest?", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-338829274", "date": "2025-03-10", "text": "Lancio questa discussione perch\u00e9 a mia sorella si \u00e8 rotto, dopo 25 anni, il frigorifero a incasso della sua cucina.Qual \u00e8 il problema? Le aziende di elettrodomestici continuano a cambiare le misure di quelli a incasso e quindi non esiste pi\u00f9 un frigorifero come il suo largo 65 cm, incassato in una colonna larga 70 cm, e la proposta \u00e8 di rifare la cucina o di mettere un frigorifero a libera installazione, che rovinerebbe una cucina molto cara e rifinita nei minimi dettagli.Purtroppo il mobiliere che aveva fatto la sua cucina non esiste pi\u00f9, l'acciaio satinato dei portelloni del frigorifero non \u00e8 pi\u00f9 prodotto, il tecnico stesso dell'assistenza ha dichiarato che non esistono pi\u00f9 frigoriferi che durano oltre 20 anni, la durata \u00e8 di circa 10 anni ed \u00e8 quanto hanno dichiarato a me i tecnici dello scaldabagno, a mia madre quelli della lavastoviglie e del frigo... io stessa avevo fatto fatica 10 anni fa a trovare un frigo a libera installazione che avesse misure simili a quello precedente, perch\u00e9 non sporgesse bloccando l'ingresso in cucina (prima era profondo 54 cm e adesso superano tutti i 60 cm di profondit\u00e0), e ho rifatto del tutto la cucina quando ho dovuto sostituire la lavastoviglie (ma avevo una cucina economica svedese, ho speso pochissimo la prima volta e dopo 14 anni ho speso di nuovo pochissimo).Che senso ha, quindi, comprare una cucina di alta gamma spendendo qualcosa come 40mila euro se dopo 10 anni, quando sei costretto a cambiare uno degli elettrodomestici, o rifai tutto oppure ti rassegni a riempire in qualche modo il buco lasciato da quello vecchio?Voi cosa ne pensate?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "rossodicina", "author_name": "Elisa", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/rossodicina", "date": "2025-03-12", "text": "Il problema dell'intercambiabilit\u00e0 degli elettrodomestici \u00e8 reale, anche a fronte di una durata inferiore e considerando la velocit\u00e0 con la quale si evolvono e vengono implementate le nuove tecnologie. Ora sono \"Smart\", con componenti fatti all'estero, normative diverse, sistemi di controllo e sicurezza di emissioni ambientali, consumi etc. Impossibile prevedere se tra 10 o 15 anni trover\u00f2 il componente intercambiabile, meglio metterlo gi\u00e0 in conto.. E' un po' come farsi fare tutti gli abiti dalla sarta e pensare che tra 15 anni il fisico e la moda sar\u00e0 perfettamente uguale e potr\u00f2 rimetterli, pu\u00f2 darsi di s\u00ec ma anche no :-) Vale la pena allora spendere soldi per i mobili cucina? Io credo che gli elettrodomestici siano un po' il motore della cucina, quindi avendo budget limitato investirei senza dubbio su questi e meno nel mobile, per\u00f2 \u00e8 anche vero che il valore del mobile lo godi subito. Una cucina low cost, per quanto ben progettata, \u00e8 meno ben rifinita e meno gradevole nei dettagli, anche meno personalizzabile (Ikea o mondo convenienza certe soluzioni non le prevede proprio). Certo che pu\u00f2 venire molto gradevole nel complesso anche al cucina low-cost, ma una cucina fatta con materiali pregiati e finiture dettagliate d\u00e0 certamente soddisfazione. E comunque se spendo 40mila euro per una cucina, non credo sia un problema se tra 15 anni devo spenderne altri 2mila per una modifica che poi mi durer\u00e0 altri 15 anni per alloggiare il frigo nuovo.. insomma quello che voglio dire \u00e8 che il mobile bello ha il suo valore intrinseco nei materiali, la realizzazione e la qualit\u00e0 complessiva, come l'abito del sarto. Poi che uno ritenga valere la pena, \u00e8 una scelta molto personale. Mi viene da dire che una cucina piccola e separata, non in open-pace per esempio, con poche personalizzazioni, pu\u00f2 essere benissimo low cost e un domani se ho problemi non ho remore a cambiare tutto e in tempi forse pi\u00f9 rapidi Aver speso invece molti soldi incentiva a modificare senza cambiare tutto, che da un punto di vista ambientale \u00e8 sicuramente meglio. Infine \u00e8 certamente una riflessione da fare al momento in cui si progetta, perch\u00e9 magari appunto si possono adottare soluzioni \"previdenti\" in certi casi e pi\u00f9 flessibili in futuro", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "kendrahhendra", "author_name": "Kendrah", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kendrahhendra", "date": "2025-03-11", "text": "Would you say your dog or cat is an emotional support animal in order to purchase a property that does not otherwise allow pets? I talked to two realtors who have suggested units in buildings that do not accept pets.  They actively encouraged me to seek out doctors who for a fee will write a letter saying I need an ESA. I will not do so.  It feels unethical to me and a slap in the face to people who actually need service dogs or ESAs for true health reasons.  It also feels like a horrible way to move into a new building where everyone will resent me for having skirted their condo/coop policy. What would you do?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jennifer-hogan285", "author_name": "Jennifer Hogan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jennifer-hogan285", "date": "2025-03-12", "text": "I worked in the humane industry where I worked with a group that provided care for animals owned by people who truly needed the support of their animals, including agoraphobics, people who were terminally ill, homeless people who need both the support and protection of their pets, people with PTSD along with service dogs who helped with physical support.  I also worked with Social Services with children who had been sexually or physically abused.   These kids often had difficulty trusting a person, but would talk to an animal.  We had several animals who were super gentle, patient lap animals that wouldn't react badly if the kids lost it, but just stayed calm and snuggled.  After working in the humane industry I went to work with San Diego Mental Health Systems. @auntthelma - To say that ESAs are simply pets is so wrong.   There are some people who abuse the system and sadly there are doctors who will write letters for anyone, but for many people suffering from chronic depression or anxiety, who have suffered some traumatic event, their ESA may be the only thing getting them through the day.   I remember during the late 80s, early 90s we had a large population of people who were diagnosed with AIDS.   People were frightened and didn't want to be around someone with AIDS.  Families and friends often abandoned them and the only living being that provided support were their cat or dog that laid on the bed with them.    One of the organizations I worked with was started when a gentleman with AIDS was hospitalized.   His landlord called his parents and they came and took his dogs and had them euthanized.   He came home from the hospital to find the only support he had had been killed.   Two weeks later he committed suicide.   We decided to create a support organization that would foster and care for animals for anyone who was terminally ill. In California there are three different designations, Emotional Support Animals, Service Animals and Psychiatric Support Animals. ESAs do not need any special training and are there simply as an emotional support for a person. SAs, like seeing eye dogs, dogs for hearing impaired, dogs that can sense seizures and those trained to assist with answering doors or retrieving things for someone with a physical disability need to be certified as a service dog / service animal (most are dogs, but there are other animals that can be certified. PSAs are a hybrid.  Most are dogs.  They may be trained to gently wake a person with PTSD when the person is having nightmares, they may be trained to remind owners to take their medications, they may be trained to press an alert if their owner is having a panic attack or harming themselves or they may apply deep pressure massage to help calm their owner. Each state has different laws regarding the rules for ESAs and PSAs.   Some states don't designate PSAs any differently than ESAs although the role and training may be different. In California a landlord must allow ESAs PSAs and SAs. It is sad that people with real needs are made to suffer because there are unethical, selfish people who abuse the system.", "images": []}}

In central Virginia, these winter protection techniques can be set up around your city's average date of first frost (say,  between October 20th and October 30th) and removed by your city's average date of last frost (say, between April 10th and April 20th). title: UPDATE: I got my new gas range (and fridge)! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "editoria", "author_name": "Alisande", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/editoria", "date": "2025-03-13", "text": "I posted in January that I was shopping for a new gas range. I mentioned that I didn't need the oven to be an air fryer, and I wasn't crazy about the trendy griddle and oval burner in the middle.  I was shopping for a refrigerator at the same time. I didn't say much about a fridge, but I also didn't want an ice maker or water dispenser. It didn't take me long to realize eliminating these features severely shrunk my options. So I adopted an \"Okay, fine\" approach and expanded my possiblities. My old appliances still worked, but I felt a little pressure because I wanted to nail down the purchases before tariffs became an issue. I finally chose two models from the Frigidaire Gallery line:  the GCRG3060BF gas range and the GRFN2023AF refrigerator. So far I'm happy with both, although I have to see about getting the burners adjusted as even the flame on the smallest \"simmer\" burner doesn't go low enough. I tried to cook rice on that one, and my pot boiled over.  So far I've used the oven (true convection) only to bake muffins, and it did a nice job. As for the fridge, it has an ice maker and water dispenser (inside), but we didn't hook them up to a water supply. Without the ice, I can make use of all the freezer space. The total capacity (20.3 cu.ft.) is a little smaller than my previous fridge (22 cu.ft.), which I noticed at first, but now it seems roomy enough. I'd worried that the LED lighting would be a pain (literally) with my photosensitivity, but I really like it. As it turned out, the only light that bothers me is the digital clock on the range. My old one wasn't a problem, but this one really glares. I can always ask Alexa what time it is instead. \ud83d\ude09 The fridge has French doors. I read a lot of opinions, both pro and con, and finally decided to get them because I like the way they look. I wanted to stick with Frigidaire Gallery to get a $200 rebate for buying two appliances, and the bottom freezer model with a single refrigerator door looked very sleek--too modernistic for my old house. When the left door is open, I can open the left crisper drawer, but in order to open the right crisper drawer I have to open both doors. Seems odd, but perhaps there wasn't a better way to do it. My house isn't the easiest to work in, but the delivery went well and the guys were great. The hardest parts were preparing for the delivery and cleaning the spaces after they took the old appliances out. I'm glad it's done, and I'm glad I'm glad my appliance shopping is done too.", "images": []}

Is there anything I can do to encourage growth on this now bare branch?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/8c126efd07d34bd0_0756-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/6922700f07d34bd2_0756-w500-h803-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "heythr23", "author_name": "heythr23", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/heythr23", "date": "2025-03-13", "text": "This bare branch forks off from the main trunk, which is hard to see in the pictures.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "webuser-355114", "author_name": "tapla  (mid-Michigan, USDA z5b-6a)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-355114", "date": "2025-03-31", "text": "Immediately above the point where the leaf attaches is a crotch called the leaf axil. There is a row of dormant buds in that axil. The growing tip of the branch produces most of a growth regulator (hormone) called auxin, which suppresses activation of the dormant buds I mentioned. Removing the branch tip (apical meristem) and the leaves having been removed should reduce auxin flow which will allow activation of the dormant buds which are obligated to become branches. A singular leaf will never again grow from the point where a singular leaf once was. Al", "images": []}}

It certainly has worked:  the onetime two-three ft. wide ditch at the crossing point is now about fifteen feet of muddy silt and flowing water, and below the crossing where the roses are, it's even wider. I would also forego the glass doors and just get regular doors. A couple of options: Option 1:  Full-depth cabinet (24\"D) and store vases and pitchers. Regardless of option, I recommend not bringing the cabinet all the way down to the top of the refrigerator. Then, slide the refrigerator in.  The end panels should be deep enough to cover the refrigerator box, not doors, and no deeper.  Deeper ones would block the movement of the doors and prevent them from opening fully. The 37\"-38\" assumes you have a 36\"W refrigerator and will never go wider.  If you think you might go wider in the future, then consider putting in a couple of 6\"W pullouts on either side of the refrigerator to give you options in the future.  However, 36\" is the most common width for refrigerators, especially counter-depth, so I don't know if you want to go any wider. title: 3 1/2 weeks in Hospital (Very long) | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "cherryfizz", "author_name": "Cherryfizz", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/cherryfizz", "date": "2025-03-14", "text": "I have been home for 10 days now after spending 3 1/2 weeks in the hospital. I had to call an ambulance in the wee hour of the morning. I started retaining fluid, felt like I gained the 100 lbs I lost, my legs, hips and abdomen were swollen. My body felt alien to me and not mine. I couldn't figure out why I was retaining fluid as I take 2 diuretics and try to reduce my sodium intake.  I was in a lot of pain from it so I took a 600 mg Ibuprofen for 2 days knowing I probably shouldn't be taking them because they can interact with blood thinners but I was in so   much pain  During those 2 days I was so weak, I could hardly walk without being short of breath or after one step needed to sit down. I couldn't even lift a bowl out of the fridge. I don't know how but I managed to do some laundry so I would have clean pjs to take with me, packed a bag because I figured they would admit me then called the ambulance. The EMTs stayed with me while I was in triage which was only an hour before I was moved into my own triage room with a bathroom.  I had blood tests, a bladder ultrasound, a rectal exam, portable chest x-ray. After they got the blood test results the Doctor asked if I was bleeding anywhere, did I have an ulcer, black stools, blood urine and I said no.  The Doctor told me it was a good thing I came in because I had a hemoglobin level of 20 which was life threatening. I had a blood transfusion then the nurse came in and took over 20 vials of blood via IV port to test for some unique Factor tests which they normally don't do.  I asked the Doctor about the water retention and he said my blood wasn't being pumped to throughout my body because of lack of oxygen. I told him about taking the ibuprofen and he said that was part of it because of the interaction with my blood thinner. The male nurse came back in to put in a catheter but he couldn't do it, so he came back with another male nurse and it took them half hour to get it to work.  You sure do lose all your modesty. After a few  hours I was moved to a 4 person ward. I was given really strong lasix by IV to help get rid of the fluid. I hated that catheter, it just didn't feel right and was painful. I have had a catheter before and didn't feel it all.  2 days later one of the nurses noticed that  I had a latex allergy and she said the nurses in triage used a latex catheter so she changed it. It was still painful and hurt. Then I noticed my urine was very dark which concerned me because it is always clear.  The nurses just said I was dehydrated because of all the fluid which is coming off me.  I always tried to get into the washroom before shift change in the am and I only needed to use the washroom twice a day so I sat in my recliner most of the day but I needed help getting our of it because it was too low. One day an ambulatory person was getting me up to go for a walk she wrenched my good arm and I lost my reach, my right arm was already bad and I can only reach backwards and can't life it.  That just made things so much worse, I felt like an invalid. One morning I was in the washroom before shift change an when I stood up I felt a pressure and a pop and as I stood up there was blood everywhere. My catheter popped out and what a relief I felt. It took a half an hour for the nurse to answer the call bell in the bathroom because the shift was changing. When they came in they were shocked at all the blood. They washed me down and put me into the bed. They stopped the lasix because there would be too much urine and would cause my bladder to spasm, they had already stopped my blood thinner. The next day another nurse came in who was a pro inserting catheters. She said she got me a new type with a larger balloon and it sure did feel so much better than the other ones. What a relief. There still was a lot of blood in the catheter bag and I knew I was bleeding somewhere. My night male nurse didn't like the look of it so was going to tell the Doctor on the floor the next morning. I already talked to the Doctor about it and he said it wasn't blood.  The next morning the Doctor came in and I asked about the dark urine and he said it wasn't blood and I asked him if  he tested it and he said yes.  That night my male nurse was back in and I told him what the Doctor said and he said my blood urine was not tested.  That Doctor lied to me! If you can't trust your Doctor who can you trust.  The next morning it was tested which showed I had a UTI which I have never had and was caused by the catheter so I was bleeding and why I was in so much pain. They hooked me up to antibiotics for the next 2 weeks and which I am still taking. My hand was painful and swollen and I just thought it was arthritis but the new Doctor coming in did some blood tests and said I had the highest level of uric acid he has ever seen. I knew I had hereditary high uric acid but not that high. I don't drink alcohol, or eat lots of red meat and rarely shrimp, no high purine vegetables and minimal sugar.  He put  me on Allopurinal that I will have to take for the res to of my life. I also had very low potassium and had to take supplements, I had 3 more blood transfusions because I was anemic. Another Doctor said I needed an iron infusion. It was so weird watching this bag of black iron mixed with glucose go into my vein. After I had it the Doctor said my colour was back in my face.  She wanted me to have an endoscopy which kind of scared me because I thought I had to be awake when they put the tube in my throat but she said no I would be in twilight sleep.  While I was in the endoscopy lab the nurses looked at my IV port and the one nurse said she wanted to go to the 5th floor to given them a piece of her mind. I had complained every day that the port was painful and had them check it. They said it was most likely the tape holding it in, but it just didn't feel right. They said it was working so should be good. The endoscopy nurse said it was infected and had to put a new one in to give me the twilight drug and she said because it would be painful she would remove the bad one after I was asleep.  After giving me the twilight drug the procedure seemed to only last a minute and I didn't feel a thing.  Towards the morning I tried to shift myself in bed I noticed my stomach was sore and achey and thought maybe they had to take a biopsy and that worried me but the Doctor said they found 2 spots that were bleeding and lasered them. I still wasn't losing enough fluid off my body and everyday I weighed myself. One day I lost 7 pounds of fluid and a few days  later gained it all back despite being on a low sodium diet. One of my Doctors said he wanted me to stay until all the fluid was off but my new Doctor wanted to release me. I said I wasn't ready to go. I lost my ability to walk on my own because not everyday they got me up to walk when I should have been walking twice a day but seldom did. My Doctor was upset with the staff about that.  I still had lots of fluid on my body, my thighs were double in size and was my stomach.  Everyone who was leaving to go home were taken for a walking test which I didn't get. I didn't know how I was going to get up my porch steps and into my house.. I have no room to use a walker in the house and I am unstable using the cane and not walking properly. I ended up hiring a patient transfer ambulance to get me home and into my house. My sofa is so low I have a hard time getting up off of it, My cousin and I worked it out and moved cushions around so I can get up on my own. She is just a little bitty thing and can't help me. I had to cancel my Doctor appointments and nuclear heart ultrasound because I can't get out of my house and down the steps.  I should have stayed there until I could walk or they should have sent me to rehab at the other hospital for a few weeks.  I know I am forgetting a few things. My nursing care by the RNs, RPNs and Nursing students were wonderful except for a few that didn't listen to me when I said something was wrong.  I don't miss being in a ward where there is no privacy. I was fortunate I could get up to use the washroom. I don't like the idea that they put men and women together in the same ward. For the first week the woman across from me was 93, she was very lucid during the day, had conversations with her family, Doctors and nurses and asked them questions but at night if she wanted something she wouldn't ring her call be instead of saying Nurse I need this, nurse I need that, nurse I am cold, nurse something is biting me. This would go on every night and we would tell her the nurse can't hear her you need to ring the bell. I thought I would lose my sanity if I heard her voice yell for the nurse.  Most times the nurse would come in and ask what was wrong and she would say okay, After she left another older woman came in, she was a fall hazard and would take the alarm off and go to the washroom by herself. One morning I went in there and the floor was so sticky my shoe stuck to the floor and came off, I  didn't know what it was and called housekeeping and even they couldn't get the stick off the floor. It happened a few more times and I realized she was peeing on the floor and because she had diabetes it was sticky.  Before I went in there I asked the nurse to make sure it was clean. It sure was an experience being in a ward when usually I am in a private room. I heard every type of unimaginable body and mouth sounds I never want to hear again.  I am still not feeling good, I almost called an ambulance again but didn't. The antibiotics are wreaking havoc with my intestines. I don't know if I should be drinking more water or less because I still am retaining a lot of fluid so much my one leg is weeping. Before I went in I had ordered 40 lip balms, lip balm holders and the hooks to give to the nurses, housekeeping, students in case I had to go back into the hospital after my last stay in December. They were thrilled with them because it is so dry in the hospital and they c nan attach the holder to their badge holders or uniforms. It was the least I could do for the good care I received. I just want to get well and not have to go into the hospital again. I came out with a UTI , not being able to walk when before I could walk, blood in my urine which now is back to normal and my left arm that isn't working right. Thanks for listening. Forgive me, I didn't proof read this.", "images": []}

title: Post Mortem on our 2 Free Spirits Cocktail Parties | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kswl3", "author_name": "Kswl", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kswl3", "date": "2025-03-15", "text": "You may remember I was planning two consecutive cocktail parties  two weeks apart featuring all alcohol-free and dealcoholized beers, wine,  and spirits.  Everything except the Athletic brand beers, which we bought at Wal Mart, was ordered online.  The spirits were from two companies:  Ritual and Zero Proof.  The wines were from Noughty and Ish (both fun little plays on words).  I had to order Heineken alcohol free beer online also as it was unavailable locally and that made it unnecessarily expensive IMO. Both parties were a great success; the first was a group of our \u201d regular\u201d friends from church, town, tennis, golf, local theater, etc.  I set up four different stations for beer, wine, margaritas, and other mixed drinks.  My nephew was visiting us for the first party and has had experience bartending, so he made many different drinks for people reluctant to try mixing their own.    Apparently very few people can mix anything other than \u201dtheir\u201d drink  and people were slow to try different things.    Nephew, DS2 (also visiting for the weekend), our wonderful party helper from the club restaurant and I mixed up different drinks and poured a little into tiny plastic shot glasses and took them around on trays for people to try.  We served different kinds of margaritas,including ones made with the regular bottled mix and with differently flavored Bartesian margarita  mixes also.  We made old fashioneds, Negronis, and \u201dregular\u201d gin and tonics, rum and coke, etc.  Our second party was a smaller group of people just from our neighborhood (my street is it\u2019s own \u201dpod,\u201d or phase of development).  We have a few people who do not drink for health reasons and a Mormon neighbor who doesn\u2019t drink for religious reasons, and they were delighted to come to such an event. To date there is no alcohol free Scotch or Vodka; so we served (alcohol-free versions of) gin, rum, bourbon , tequila, vermouth and campari.  In addition we served several shrubs, which are fruit-infused simple syrups (made with sugar, honey, agave, etc) mixed with vinegar (fruit vinegars, balsamics, champagne orother wine vinegars, etc).  I purchased from 1821 in Atlanta a blood orange and ginger shrub and an apple cardamom variety, and on my own made batches of pineapple/ginger/cardamom and peach/vanilla/nutmeg shrubs.  We also had on hand wonderful mixers from Withco, one called Ellis Old Fashioned (simple syrup infused with citrus and spice) and  another called Bouquet (lavender, rose and other botanicals) that were quite popular.  We also had the range of club soda, tonic waters (regular and diet for the diabetics), ginger ales and other sodas. Overall the Lavender Margaritas my nephew made were in high demand at the first party and we almost ran out of tequila.  I\u2019m not exactly sure how he made them but he was doing a brisk business shaking and pouring at the margarita station. The next most popular drink was a sparkling white wine from Ish mixed with Ellis Old Fahioned Mixer and tonic water.  This drew high praise from everyone and I am planning to use it as a signature drink at our next party.  Of the wines, the reds were abysmal but the Ish Chardonnay was drinkable, especially with a meal.  The sparkling whites and ros\u00e9s were not really good enough as a standalone but surprisingly good as a base for a cocktail.   The surprise hit was a Negroni-ish cocktail I devised with gin, vermouth, campari and a decent splash of tonic with a squeeze of orange.   One bourbon drinker mixed his bouron with the blood orange and ginger shrub and was very pleased with it.  We also had a very good reception of the rum and apple cardamom shrub with a splash of soda.   The beer drinkers were not vocal about the beers they drank so I assume they were not much enjoyed, although I have it on very good authority that the no alcohol Heineken tastes exactly like the regular type.  I wondered if our particular beer drinkers were missing the reason they drink it.  Several people commented that it was odd to drink without \u201dfeeling\u201d it and that it was a new experience they welcomed.  No one disavowed alcohol as a result of the parties and of course that was not the reason for having them, but everyone had a great time and there  was no concern about anyone getting home safely. On the food front, the standout item was the zuccini blossoms stuffed with marscapone and herbs, battered and fried, from the club\u2019s appetizer menu.  Our party helper (one of the club waitresses) came directly from her shift and brought the food with her piping hot and crispy.  We kept them  in a warm oven and Lisa put them on a platter as everyone arrived.  They were a huge hit!  I did an antipasto tray, baked brie with blackberry jam and toasted walnuts with crostini, a few other cheeses and crackers, a veggie tray (blanched green beans, cherry tomatoes and celery) with homemade ranch dip, and fruit skewers.  I also had coffee service set up in the dining room with small finger desserts (pecan bars, brownies, salted caramel brownies, lemon bars and raspberry bars) from my favorite caterer in town; she\u2019s been making those for decades and everybody loves them.  The weather was lovely for both parties, the 2/28 one a bit cooler and the one last night warmer but windier.  We were able to use the screened porch for both events and at the first were able to enjoy a spectacular sunset from the porch and windows all across the back of the house. I love to entertain and even though it seems people are having fewer parties they still like being invited to them!", "images": []}

Those single flower buds should be left alone to finish their bloom cycle. To get a maximum bud set for the second flush try this.  At dead heading time, cut back down the stem a good bit lower than the first 5 leaflet leaf to a thicker place on the cane.  The resulting lateral growths that appear will be huskier, and can be minimized/thinned per cane as they reach about an inch of growth to make the remaining growths even more  husky.  Just rub the smaller and too numerous growths right off.  Those remaining laterals left will get all the bush's energy, and should produce the maximum number of buds per variety for your second flush without any further intervention. That's about all you can do to get the maximum number of buds per stem. Still keep up proper watering and fertilizing. If you nip those single buds now, all you will get is weak new growth from the upper, currently dormant leaf node buds that are triggered to grow.  Many new growths from those leaf node buds that emerge below the nipped flower bud will be blind growths, and/or produce growths with  very small subsequent flowers on the growths that produce flower buds. main_question: {"author_id": "chloebud", "author_name": "chloebud", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/chloebud", "date": "2025-03-16", "text": "In honor of today being National Artichoke Hearts Day I thought some of you might like to share favorite recipes involving artichokes in any way/shape/form. This is one of mine l've shared more than once, but it\u2019s such a favorite. Courtesy of Jeff Smith (Frugal Gourmet).  I added a couple tweaks I make following the recipe. Lamb and Artichoke Stew From Jeff Smith - \"I have just this minute realized that writing cookbooks is much harder for me than I would have ever imagined. It is hard not because I have to explain myself, but because I have to think about these recipes, and it is not even close to lunchtime. This lamb and artichoke stew from Greece cause me particular pain. You must make this! You must!\" 4 Tbsp. butter2 pounds boneless lamb, cubed (leg or shoulder)3 yellow onions, peeled and chopped2 cloves garlic, crushed1/2 cup parsley, choppedSalt/Pepper, to taste1 (6 oz.) can tomato paste1 cup dry white wine2 (14 oz.) cans artichoke hearts in brine (not marinated), drained1/2 tsp. dried dill weed3 Tbsp. lemon juice Directions: In a large Dutch oven melt the butter. Add the lamb and saute until lightly browned. Remove the meat. Saute the yellow onions along with the garlic and parsley. Place the meat, onions, garlic, and parsley in a heavy kettle, and add salt, pepper, and the tomato paste, and white wine. Simmer, covered, for about 1 1/2 hours or until the lamb is tender. main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2025-03-17", "text": "One person on the forum said she enjoyed my posts, and that's encouragement enough. At the farm, spring has sprung.  Down at the bottom of the big garden this morning, I was enjoying the sight of the mature photinia, leathery green foliage with red new growth, and beside it Berberis julianae, small semi-glossy leaves with an occasional scarlet one for contrast, and clusters of small yellow blooms.  It's as handsome a shrub as a person could ask for, dense and rounded, but my word! those thorns.  Mine is about ten feet wide and five feet tall, probably in place for fifteen years or so.  On the other side of the drainage, pink Japanese quince, forsythia, and white Japanese quince in bloom, with a Viburnum x burkwoodii getting ready to flower.  These shrubs have the rare advantage of access to the water and nutrients of the drainage ditch, and it shows.  The roses at the bottom of the ditch in the delta are alive and for the most part look thriving.  Likewise the nettles which grow all along the ditch. Close by are the herbaceous peonies of the Peony Walk, although this is an ambitious name.  The peonies are all alive, even the one growing in sodden ground, and the two P. peregrina I transplanted last fall are sprouting vigorously.  I've been clearing the grass away from around them, a good chance to look around and see what's going on.  I'm pondering further planting of trees and shrubs for fruit in this area--it's a kind of orchard--and more peonies, too.  My feeling is that this area is going to take more time, work, and plants to reach maturity. The two tree peonies I grew from seed and the cutting-grown Viburnum x burkwoodii further up the garden are all alive and either growing (the peonies) or blooming (the viburnum).  All three are tiny.  I decided to set the peonies out, notwithstanding they were an inch tall, because they weren't growing in their pots.  The viburnum was probably mere impatience.  The area looks sadly torn up now, but will recover, and I hope will look more complete, handsome:  in a word, right. Down in the shade garden (but this is true of all the garden) is a lot of uncompleted work.  I was busy there for a few weeks doing cleanup, but got distracted by the state of the delta.  The bay laurel that had gotten totally out of hand is one branch of away from being completely cut back; the two yew hedges still must be pruned.  I did plant the three small photinias to edge the basin, accomplished a great deal of weeding, and cut back the pyracantha hedge, an awful job.  NEVER plant a pyracantha hedge, and particularly never follow that up by letting climbing roses scramble through it. 'Vanity', the rose in question, looks good, though. The crown of the willow that came down in our December snow, but got hung up, is still hung up, in spite of a lot of branches I sawed off to clear it, and sawing through the part of the crown that was still connected.  I wasn't able to lever it free; it will just have to wait until a strong enough wind brings it down.  The willow branches came in handy for some embryonic terracing I started higher up.  I haven't cleared away the broken-off branches of flowering ash that ended up on top of the pergola that houses the double white Lady Banks rose, nor finished cutting back the rose itself, though I tried to make sure it won't overwhelm 'Dupontii' further down.  'Alberic Barbier' has traveled from its hedge over to the line of flowering ashes and is climbing into them.  Clearly I have learned nothing from my experiences with 'Lady Banks'. There's plenty more going on, but this is enough for now.", "images": []}

title: Spring has sprung - at least here . . . | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "tinam1962", "author_name": "Tina Marie", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/tinam1962", "date": "2025-03-17", "text": "Spring has sprung here although today we are experiencing cool temps.  It's that time of early spring where the days are up and down.  There has been flooding in surrounding areas and we've had two episodes of crazy winds.  This past weekend there was a tornado in a county an hour or so away from us.  I have spring fever like crazy (and all the sneezing lol)!  Even the cooler days have (mostly) been gorgeous!  My candy tuft, bradford pears and tulip tree are all at full bloom.  I know it's still early, but I am looking for each new bloom.  Our creeping phlox is just starting to bloom.  Trees are budding out, clematis and other plants are shooting up out of the ground and slowly growing.  I bought a second \"Sweet Autumn\" clematis last year that I never planted in the ground.  I will transplant that soon out front.  We have one on a trellis out back.  My climbing hydrangea (which really does not look like a hydrangea at all), did great through the winter.  Temps are supposed to be up again tomorrow and much of the week, so I will be out pruning roses.  My husband has already pruned the hydrangea (huge).  Sadly, there is some crazy purple blooming weed (I never can remember it's name) that is all over so weeding must start too.  The japanese maples will be trimmed up a bit.  Soon it will be time to plant my pots.  I can't wait!   I also can't wait for the dogwoods - that will be a few more weeks.  We have a \"Dogwood Arts Festival\" next month.  We will be heading further south in a few weeks and I know we'll see more blooms along the way.  It's my favorite time of year!   : )    How about you? title: Hausbau mit 3 Kindern und Großeltern | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-621973838", "author_name": "Andr\u00e9 Wentzel", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-621973838", "date": "2025-03-18", "text": "Hallo zusammen Ich bin wahnsinnig begeistert, was f\u00fcr tolle R\u00fcckmeldungen ich in den Kommentaren lese und w\u00fcrde euch gerne unser Bauvorhaben vorstellen und euch einladen zu Feedback, kritischen Kommentaren oder Verbesserungsvorschl\u00e4gen. Wir sind eine 5-k\u00f6pfige Famile: 2 Erwachsene und drei (zum Zeitpunkt des Einzuges etwa) 4 J\u00e4hrige Kinder (Drillinge). Zus\u00e4tzlich werden unsere Schwiegereltern nebenan wohnen. Somit w\u00e4ren wir zu 7. aus unserem Grundst\u00fcck: Wir 5 in einem Einfamilienhaus (2 Geschosse mit Kniestock und Keller), und die 2 Gro\u00dfeltern in einem eigenen Bungalow (mit einem kleinen Kellerraum, ansonsten Bodenplatte). Wir bauen in Holzst\u00e4nderbauweise mit einem Fertighausanbieter. Wir sind kurz vor der Vertragsunterschrift und finden den Grundriss soweit gut und w\u00fcrden diesen zum aktuellen Zeitpunkt so umsetzen. Vielleicht inspieriert uns hier aber noch was, was uns die n\u00e4chsten 30 Jahre jeden Tag das Leben vereinfacht oder versch\u00f6nert :) Herausforderung des Grundst\u00fccks: - Es ist schmal geschnitten - S\u00fcd-Nord Ausrichtung, also Garten zur Stra\u00dfe hin Gr\u00f6\u00dfte W\u00fcnsche an das neue Zuhause EFH: - K\u00fcche und Esszimmer sollen der Lebensmittelpunkt sein - Viel nat\u00fcrliches Licht - keine beengenden R\u00e4ume oder Flure - 3 Kinderzimmer - 1 Elternschlafzimmer mit Ankleide und Masterbad - f\u00fcr die Kinder ein Kinderbad - ein G\u00e4ste-WC im EG - Sitzfenster Gr\u00f6\u00dfte W\u00fcnsche an das neue Zuhause ELW: - Ebenerdig - 2 Schlafzimmer (er schnarcht laut - ihr werdet euch sicherlich auch fragen, ob die Schiebet\u00fcr und die Wand dazwischen reichen um das zu verstummen - ich wei\u00df es selbst noch nicht) - ein G\u00e4ste-WC - Speisekammer (nicht ersichtlich, aber dort ist auch WM und Trockner untergebracht) Zum EFH: Wir h\u00e4tten gerne einen klassischen Grundriss, im Sinne von Essen und Wohnen unten, Schlafen oben. Das EG erh\u00e4lt eine 20cm Geschosserh\u00f6hung. Im G\u00e4ste-WC hatten wir urspr\u00fcnglich eine Dusche geplant und dann aber empfunden, dass uns die gr\u00f6\u00dfere Speisekammer mehr Komfort bringt. Wann duscht schon mal jemand im EG im Verh\u00e4ltnis zum Nutzen der Speisekammer. Falls ich mir ein Bein gebrochen habe oder keine Treppensteigen kann, wird mir das vielleicht fehlen, aber ich werde vermutlich die Treppen schon irgendwie hochkommen. Zus\u00e4tzlich m\u00f6chte ich nicht immer alle M\u00f6glichkeiten miteinplanen und dann 90% der Zeit nicht nutzen. G\u00e4ste sollen bei uns dann im Kinderbad duschen. Zum Punkt G\u00e4ste: Diese sollen im B\u00fcro auf einer Schlafcouch untergebracht werden. Aktuell haben wir etwa 1x alle 2-3 Monate einen \u00dcbernachtungsgast. Kinderg\u00e4ste sollen bei denen im Zimmer \u00fcbernachten. In der Diele haben wir eine Garderobe vor dem Treppenaufgang geplant. Unter der Treppe wird eine T\u00fcr angebracht, die dann in den Keller f\u00fchrt (T\u00fcr wegen KfW 40). Der Durchgang zur K\u00fcche und in den Essen/Wohnen-Bereich soll offen sein. Die K\u00fcche ist so gew\u00fcnscht wie abgebildet. Meiner Frau war der Ausblick an der Sp\u00fcle wichtig. Aktuell ist noch ein Kamin eingezeichnet, den wir aber gestrichen haben. Wir planen hier einen Elektrokamin, der einfach nur f\u00fcr Ambiente sorgt. Also der Platz ist vielleicht dann auch vergeben, aber es muss kein Schornstein und alles weitere (Holz-Lagerplatz, usw.) ber\u00fccksichtigt werden. Nach drau\u00dfen geht es dann \u00fcber eine Hebeschiebet\u00fcre. Aktuell ist noch 2,92m eingezeichnet, diese wird aber auf 3,42m vergr\u00f6\u00dfert und das festverglaste Fenster daneben wird gestrichen. Das geht auf Kosten der Symmetrie mit den Fenstern im OG (ersichtlich in der West-Ansicht), vielleicht werden wir aber die Hebeschiebet\u00fcre nochmals um 50cm verbreitern, da wei\u00df ich den Mehrpreis noch nicht. Ich k\u00f6nnte mir vorstellen, dass es dann wieder mit dem Fenster aus dem OG passt. Wenn man rauskommt und zur ELW schaut, soll dort an das vorstehende Eck ein Schuppen angrenzen, f\u00fcr die Gartenger\u00e4te. Die Terrasse der ELW wird auch nochmals nach hinten verschoben und zwischen Terrasse ELW und Schuppen soll dann eine Treppe in ihren Kellerraum f\u00fchren. Jetzt wieder zum EFH :) Der Garten soll mit min. 1,20m Zaun eingez\u00e4unt werden, da wir einen grossen Hund haben, der \u00fcber einen niedrigeren Zaun ohne Probleme springt. Die Garage ist als Doppelgarage eingezeichnet, davon sind wir aber abgekommen. Wir besitzen nur ein Auto und h\u00e4tten gerne eine Einzelgarage (vermutlich \u00fcberwiegend f\u00fcr Fahrr\u00e4der und andere Ger\u00e4te) und ein angebautes Carport f\u00fcr unser Auto. So kann aus dem K\u00fcchenfenster auch mehr beobachtet, \u00e4hhh... erblickt werden ;). Das Auto der Gro\u00dfeltern soll dann auf dem links vom Weg zum Haus eingezeichneten Caport-Platz stehen. Auch das ist ein relativ weiter weg f\u00fcr \u00e4ltere Menschen, lies sich aber anders nicht l\u00f6sen. Alles nach links zu schieben und nach hinten fahren war f\u00fcr uns zu unsicher (ihr aktuelles Auto haben sie sich leider auch schon total an einer Hauswand aufgerissen). Die M\u00fclleimer m\u00f6chten wir hinter unserer L-Haust\u00fcr\u00fcberdachung unterbringen, sodass sie von der Stra\u00dfe her und wenn man zum Haus l\u00e4uft nicht ersichtlich sind. In unseren beiden B\u00e4den wird es noch Umstrukturierungen geben, da unsere Dusche in der Schr\u00e4ge steht und ich gerne das WC der Kinder zum Fenster hin gerichtet h\u00e4tte (aufgrund der besseren Abluft :)). Zudem soll das Dach vom Bungalow (ELW) von der Ankleide aus begehbar gemacht werden. Dort h\u00e4tten wir in der Zukunf die M\u00f6glichkeit eine Aussensauna oder \u00e4hnliches zu platzieren. Letzter Punkt: Keller. Wir planen einen Kellerraum f\u00fcr Technik, einen Raum f\u00fcr W\u00e4sche mit WM, Trockner und W\u00e4schest\u00e4nder (dort kommt auch der W\u00e4scheabwurf raus) und ein Raum welcher aufgeteilt ist in Stauraum und Fitnessraum. Vielleicht braucht es dort noch eine Raumtrennung (das ist der Keller Hobby). Kommen wir zur ELW: Der Eingang wird hier durch ein \u00fcberstehendes Dach des Bungalows gesch\u00fctzt sein. Der Schlaf- und Hygienebereich der Gro\u00dfeltern soll abgetrennt und nicht einsehbar sein. Deshalb haben sie ihr Schlafen, Ankleide und Bad abgetrennt. Ein G\u00e4ste-WC soll es geben, damit der Bereich auch abgetrennt bleiben darf. Der Fokus soll auch in diesem Haus auf der K\u00fcche und dem Esszimmer liegen. Es ist eine Kochinsel unbedingt gew\u00fcnscht. Die T\u00fcr zur Speisekammer hintenraus ist z.B. f\u00fcr das rausstellen/aufh\u00e4ngen von W\u00e4sche gedacht. Sie haben auch eine Hebeschiebet\u00fcre und eine kleine Terrasse. Geplant ist grunds\u00e4tzlich, dass sie viel bei uns sein werden. Wir werden sehen wie das dann in der Realit\u00e4t ist. Der Schuppen bei ihnen ist mal eingezeichnet, hat aber noch keine gro\u00dfe Priorit\u00e4t. Grunds\u00e4tzlich noch zur Gartengestaltung: Damit die Kinder einen sch\u00f6nen Garten zum Spielen haben, planen wir unsere Terrasse nur bis zur Kante der Haus-S\u00fcdseite zu verlegen, dann aber bis nach links zur Grundst\u00fccksgrenze und auch bis nach hinten, zur Kante von der ELW. Dann haben die Kinder (und auch wir gro\u00dfen Kinder :)) eine gr\u00f6\u00dfere Fl\u00e4che f\u00fcr Rasen, Fu\u00dfballtore oder B\u00e4ume. Die eingezeichnete Terrassen\u00fcberdachung haben wir jetzt gestrichen. Das werden wir bauseits vermutlich mit einer an das Haus angebauten Pergola l\u00f6sen. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "outpaientzero", "author_name": "outpaientzero", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/outpaientzero", "date": "2025-03-18", "text": "I use and presently have cases of Mylar bags.  There is nothing which comes close to keeping oxygen, moisture and LIGHT out except glass jars protected from all light.  Real Mylar consists of three layers, a layer of plastic on the inside and outside and nothing special, but a sheet of Aluminum foil sandwiched in between the plastic giving them the ability to nearly stop any oxygen, moisture and light from passing through.  There are other bags made called Mylar but the center layer is sprayed on and not nearly as effective.  The aluminum is sprayed on and not actual foil, and have no idea how they make either.You may have the sprayed on foil bags in your house right now and are used for packaging shacks and chips, like fritos and poptarts.  When opened They'll have a silver color but over that silver is a clear food grade plastic.  To tell the difference a flashlight will shine through the sprayed on bags but real Mylar will allow no light to pass.For a comparison a real 5 mil thick heat sealed Mylar bag will keep moisture, oxygen and light out for at about 42 years before equalizing without an oxygen absorber to the outside environment, with an absorber it could take over 100 years.  A sealed food saver bag will keep out moisture and oxygen for about 10 years before equalizing, and a zip lock freezer bag will only last about 2 weeks because of the zipper. title: Please help! Shower tile gone wrong. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jackie-c91", "author_name": "J C", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jackie-c91", "date": "2025-03-20", "text": "I bought tile not knowing it varied in color. when I went to Lowes and looked in the box the first rows were the same. It was not until the tile installer was almost finished that I realized there were different variations in color\u2026and it was too late. I asked why no one consulted me on how I wanted the tile laid out before starting. The GC (hired sub-contractors) was not present and he said they normally just pull them from the box. They refuse to redo the job unless I pay more money. How is this acceptable? Am I crazy?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/0f52dc2f07db81bb_8850-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dani-m08", "author_name": "dani_m08", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dani-m08", "date": "2025-03-21", "text": "This appears to be the tile that was purchased at Lowe's:   It apparently has three different shades of tile.  It is also listed as a V2 shade variation = slight variation - I was surprised to see it listed as a V2.   The three shades that it shows on the website appear to not be as dramatically different as the shades of tile on your walls:   It is also sold by the piece vs. box - which causes issues at big box stores because people can purchase many boxes of the tile - then sort through them at home (some people actually sorted through them in the actual store - I'm surprised that the store allowed them to do that) in order to only keep the pieces that they want - and return all of the ones they don't want. So, if you opened a box of tile at the store, it may have been a returned box = someone didn't want a particular shade of the tile - which made you think that the rest of the boxes would contain that particular shade = be pretty consistent in color. When people posted a comment about doing the above on this forum,  it always involved natural stone tile (specifically marble) - but I'm sure that it happens with other tile (although, I don't understand why they didn't just purchase a different tile instead). I've read comments on this forum where people have explained how they bought their marble tile at Lowe's/HD - and sorted through the tile in order to remove all of the pieces that they didn't like (weird rust color/green veins/darker background/etc).  The problem is that the price of the marble tile is set based upon the level of quality - when people sort through a ton of boxes in order to select only tiles with lighter backgrounds + nice veining, they've now received $50 per sf marble tile instead of the $6-8 per sf tile that they purchased. If another customer doesn't look through all of their boxes of tile PRIOR to installation - they wind up coming home to find a very different looking marble shower surround than they were expecting (based upon the sample board at the store).  Basically, they have a shower that was made out of rejected tile. If a homeowner has a designer - the homeowner would be able to rely on receiving a call + texts showing the tile.  Also, if a designer knew that the tile was a V2 - slight variation tile, but saw the tile you received, he/she would have contacted you to discuss the issue (after all, you would be paying client that he/she would want to make happy + the designer wouldn't want his/her name connected to a project that didn't turn out as expected).  A designer also would have specified the installation pattern. Also, if the homeowner had an experienced tile professional (TCNA or CTI certified) doing the installation, while they shouldn't rely on the installer to notify them, the installer would most likely make a call and/or send some photos in order to confirm that the quality (or the drastic color variation) was what the homeowner was expecting. main_question: {"author_id": "joseph-corlett-llc-pfvwus-pf~848525206", "author_name": "Joseph Corlett, LLC", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/general-contractors/joseph-corlett-llc-pfvwus-pf~848525206", "date": "2025-03-21", "text": "ZepBound I\u2019ve never been a fat guy. I was 5\u2019 8\u201d and 168 pounds a little over a decade ago, but on a recent checkup I\u2019ve apparently shrunk an inch and gained 20 pounds. This isn\u2019t my idea of aging gracefully and at 69, I\u2019ve still got some fight left in me. I heard that ZepBound (tirzepatide), was the only weight loss drug approved for the treatment of sleep apnea, from which I suffer. I had an Inspire machine imbedded into my chest several years ago. They connect a wire to your lungs and tongue and when the battery pack gets the signal that you\u2019re not breathing, it jolts your tongue into the proper position while you sleep. If you\u2019re too overweight, you\u2019re ineligible for the machine. It sure beats wearing that damn nasty mask. My sleep doctor prescribed it, the 20 extra pounds making me eligible by bumping my Body Mass Index just into qualification. The pharmacy auto call told me it was ready and that my share of the bill would be just over $900.00 for a 1-month supply. Damn. I thought since this was prescribed for sleep apnea instead of weight loss that Medicare was going to pick up the tab. The pharmacist suggested I make a claim with my secondary insurance. I thought, \u201cYeah, right\u201d, but I made the claim and damned if they didn\u2019t approve it! I paid the $600.00 yearly deductible feeling like I got a deal. I\u2019m not a big fan of needles, but sitting at my kitchen table with my thigh cleaned and exposed, I twisted the top off the ZepBound injector, placed it on my thigh, turned the safety off, hit the button ,and got what felt like a bug bite with a tiny bloody dot afterward. I\u2019ve done 3 weekly injections so far, and with the exception of some mild heartburn, haven\u2019t experienced any side effects. I read the pamphlet. None of those scared me except for possible hair loss, however, this stuff does what it claims to do. You just don\u2019t want to eat. At a luncheon at a high school class reunion last week, I was served a nice, not too big/not too small portion of chicken linguine. I hadn\u2019t had breakfast. It was delicious. The old me would have snarfed that plate; no problem. I finished just over half and couldn\u2019t have eaten another bite if you\u2019d paid me. The 5 classmates at my table cleaned their plates. I ate the rest the next day. Yesterday I had two small pieces of buttered toast for breakfast, half a Reuben sandwich for lunch, and no hunger or food the rest of the day. Another advantage is ZepBound reduces your alcohol cravings. I wouldn\u2019t describe myself as a raging alcoholic, but 3 glasses of Chardonnay after dinner wasn\u2019t unusual. If I get with a certain gang of friends, you know who you are, I\u2019ll sip wine all night and with sleep apnea, I\u2019m not really supposed to do that or nap. Two nights ago, I had a beer with lunch and one in the evening. The night before last, one Chardonnay and done. Nothing last night, but I\u2019m having dinner with the crowd my mother warned me about tonight, so all bets are off. I slept really well last night, so I\u2019ve got to at least quit early even if I don\u2019t abstain. I\u2019ve been off caffeine for 30 years at doctor\u2019s orders, but there\u2019s no way I could have written this without a half caf coffee, despite last night\u2019s rest. Continuing my aging fight, I\u2019ve managed to coral my needle fear long enough to have Botox injections eliminate my forehead wrinkles and crow\u2019s feet, but that damn deductible ruined my vanity budget for the month. The downside is you can\u2019t facially express surprise anymore, but with the way the country and world are going, nothing surprises me anymore anyway. Speaking of vanity, I wasn\u2019t vain enough to pay my eye surgeon the nine thousand dollars he wanted to do my lower eyelids while he was doing my uppers that Medicare paid for. Medicare pays for vision, not vanity, which is just a very nice side effect. I could fly to South Korea, they lead the world in cosmetic surgery, get my uppers and lowers done, hotel, hookers, and home for less than nine large. I checked. I also checked into the hair transplant leader of the world, Turkey. They\u2019ll do state of the art hair transplants for about ten times less than stateside, but my budget and vanity are duking that one out. I\u2019m passing for now. I get Testosterone Replacement Therapy from my urologist who keeps an eye, and a gloved finger, on my prostate. None of that late night television bottled junk that isn\u2019t approved by the FDA, I\u2019m talking about timed pellets stitched under the skin of your hip every 3 months. Medicare pays. Yes, it increases and/or maintains your sex drive and while I know correlation isn\u2019t causation, I haven\u2019t gotten the blues since I started. I bought a microwave oven at the used appliance store and while digging through my toolbox to install it, I found a hearing aid I\u2019d lost several years ago that cost me $250.00 to replace. Now I\u2019ve got a backup. I\u2019m not crazy about my hearing aids, but my phone app lets me turn down background noise which is critical when I\u2019m reading to my pre-k kids as a volunteer or hanging with my loud friends. I am considering switching to Sebo but don't know anything about the brand.   My reference point is Miele.  Quality-wise, is Sebo on par with Miele?  What features do you like or don't like on the Sebo? My requirements are:  (1) canister style, and (2) power head attachment.  Beyond that, I want a unit as compact and light as possible.  The guy at the vacuum store said the Sebo K3 is the most compact and lightest that has my requirements, and in the Miele the C1 or the C3 styles.   I \"kicked the tires\" at the vacuum store the other day when I took my old gal in for repair, and I do like the head on the Sebo better, but weight-wise they're all about the same.  We didn't get into all the different features -- will do that and test them when I go back. Anyway, I think mainly what I'm looking for here is input on Sebo canisters and if you have experience with both Miele and Sebo a comparison.  Thanks!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mxk3", "author_name": "porkchop_z5b_MI", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mxk3", "date": "2025-03-22", "text": "(Long) Update: Well, I ended up buying a Sebo E3. I compared the different models and features between the Miele and Sebo at the vacuum store.  While there are some things I like better on the Miele, the Sebo was less expensive for a comparable machine and I like the hose handle much better. The hose handle on the Sebo isn't as thick in circumference and it bends at a more natural angle so it's more comfortable in the hand. That wasn't a deal-breaker on the Miele - after all, I was used to it. What made the difference for me is the suction control is on the handle of the Sebo, rather than on the canister itself, so if you're going from one situation to another where you need to adjust the suction, you don't have to stop, turn around, reach down and fiddle with the controls on the Miele. I also like the size and shape of the power head on the Sebo better -- my my the power heads on Miele are HUGE now, and they're bulky. I also thought the pedal to unlock the head out of the upright position was very awkward on the Miele; with the Sebo it's a simple foot pedal like an upright, but the Miele you kind of have to push the wand forward and then push backward on the pedal and it's on the top of the \"hood\" of the head -- it's just weird, I didn't like that at all. My old machine didn't have a pedal at all, it just moved into the \"I'm vacuuming now\" position with a simple arm motion moving the wand downwards. What I don't like as much about the Sebo compared to the Miele is that the power cord mechanism is encased in plastic along the backside of the metal wand -- I don't really know how the power gets down to the head of the Miele, but there's no plastic encasement, the wand is just a metal tube and is more comfortable to grip if you need to grip the wand for some reason. I also like the larger parquet head on the Miele better and the fact that it easily swivels to get tightly along the baseboards (well, mine did anyway); the Sebo parquet head is narrower front to back, and it kinda sorta swivels but it takes some effort. I'll have to look into whether they have a different size I can buy. I also don't like how the duster attachment attaches to the front of the wand, kind of like a big protruding medallion on the wand, it was bugging me when I was going under the furuniture so I ended up taking it off and putting it in the closet. Not a big deal since I don't use that attachment much, but that seems like it could be better thought out, since the beauty of a canister is its manueverability under furniture and around tight spaces and this thing just gets in the way IMO. This new power head is definitely going to take some getting used to. It definitely has some power to it, it wants to pull me along -- it's almost like a self-propelled upright feels. That is much different than my old Miele, but in fairness it was an old machine and I imagine technology and components are much improved in the last quarter-century... It feels like this new power head has a mind of its own and wants to get away from me, but I'm sure I'll get used to it after an adjustment period. Oh, and this machine has a power cord that is a fair length longer than the cord on my old machine, which was a pleasant surprise, I can now get all the way down the hall and into the bathroom with the thing without changing outlets. Now, I've only used it once, but so far so good -- have to get used to the new but it did suck up all the dog hair off the hardwood effortlessly and the power head seems to have cleaned the doors mats well, so far so good. :0)", "images": []}}

When I first got this plant it reliably stayed evergreen for the first few years but it started going dormant for the winter 2 years ago. Anyone know what may be happening?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/61b2a43407df93eb_5647-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "suzy-jackson88", "author_name": "suzy jackson", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/suzy-jackson88", "date": "2025-03-23", "text": "By 'evergreen' this does not mean always and perpetually in leaf. All evergreens shed foliage, just at different times and quantities than deciduous plants which have a much more prolonged dormancy and a tendency to lose all foliage at once, for months instead of continuous foliage replacement over a whole season (such as my bay trees) or for a few weeks while new foliage is rapidly replaced (such as hellebores). Of course, this is my entirely unscientific observations but I have yet to see any plant which retains all it's foliage with no obvious signs of replacement.
