title: Do you have a color of roses that you find yourself avoiding? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "nippstress", "author_name": "nippstress - zone 5 Nebraska", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nippstress", "date": "2025-03-24", "text": "Hi folks For starters, I have roses in every color I can imagine so it's not that I avoid any color entirely. I definitely seek out some colors - the russets, true lavender, stripes and other oddballs particularly. Lately as I'm filling in some holes, I notice a trend of rose colors that have to be extra special to pique my interests. Before I started rose gardening, I would have predicted that orange would be the color I hated since I can't stand it around me in my house or clothes. However, the \"zing\" of orange roses has captivated me enough to have roses like Cary Grant on my wish lists (plus the name...) and to have sections of my \"hot colors\" bed brightened up with orange. I think it's the large palette of a garden bed that makes orange roses appealing to me. It would be hard to be a rose gardener without at least tolerating pink, since so many roses either start there, fade to pink, or have pink tones to their white. If you appreciate old garden roses, pink and white are go-to colors. As I'm reviewing available roses now that I don't have wide-open spaces to fill, I find that I tend to do a quicker cut of yellow roses than other colors for wish lists. I have my share of true yellow roses like Mellow Yellow, Shockwave (didn't survive my winters tho) or Lichtkonigen Lucia, but my yellow choices tend to emphasize cream (like Teasing Georgia or Lunar Mist) or apricot (like Melissa Darling, Tupelo Honey or Easy Going). I have Julia Child and she does OK but fades to a mucky sort of cream in my yard so that she's not a favorite. I know Diane will chime in to tempt me with her gorgeous JC photos, but I don't think mine is ever going to achieve those heights of glory. In general I don't find that yellows hold my interest (or their color) long enough to be a favorite. I don't avoid them actively, but if I only have so much room on my wish list the yellow roses can be the first ones cut. I can handle the pinks that fade to cream because it tends to be a nicer cream than the way many yellows fade. Just me I'm sure! What do you find might be less than ideal colors for you? Just curious Cynthia", "images": []}

In certain lighting, they might look the same. Just make sure you think they look pretty together you don't want it to look like the intention was color drenching but the match is off. LRV has one job\u2014and it\u2019s not a very useful one when it comes to paint and color. All it tells you is how much light a color reflects. That\u2019s it. LRV has nothing to do with whiteness, and that\u2019s an important distinction and this is a good example. Because Cheviot has more Chroma - or could say it's more colorful so more of its yellow hue parent is discernible. And it's that extra yellowness that makes Cheviot more reflective and higher in LRV. Bottom line, LRV is not useful; it doesn't describe what a color looks like in anyway shape or form and in this case it's super unhelpful. What is helpful is LCh. Don't have to understand the jargon or the numbers (data values) to get just how similar Cheviot and Snowbound are. L = Lightness (how light/dark a color looks) C = Chroma (strong/weak how neutral or colorful a color looks) h = Hue Angle (a color's hue family)", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/a3d296ce07e3cc65_2249-w240-h135-b0-p0--.jpg"]}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "anneannahs", "author_name": "anneannahs", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/anneannahs", "date": "2025-03-26", "text": "Thank you!", "images": []}}

There are five kinds of slot shelving hardware: 1. 1\" on center (one inch from the centers of adjacent slots). These are commonly used in homes. 2. 2\" on center. These are used in commercial applications, such as display shelves in stores. 3 & 4. 1\" and 2\" on center dual track. These have two parallel rows of slots on each standard. 5. The ones in my workshop. They're 2\" OC single slot, but they aren't compatible with standard 2\" OC hardware. When I bought some \"standard\" 2\" OC brackets and tried to install them, they hit the wall before they could engage the slots. I tried them on a standard that I removed from the wall, and they still didn't fit. They're designed for longer slots. My standards are 13/16\" wide and 15/32\" deep (face of standard to wall). The slots are 3/16\" wide and 29/32\" long. The brackets are inserted by pushing them straight into the slots and down, unlike the \"standard\" 2\" OC brackets, which you apparently tilt up,  insert into the upper slot, lower to horizontal, and push down. And TikTok for that matter. I love to watch videos of food garden tours and I also love TikToks where the gardeners go out into their gardens and harvest their goodies for the day. Well, this also tends to make me think! OH! I want that in MY garden! Every year I always find SOMETHING new (to me) that I want to try to grow. So far, these wild ideas have not been successful. I am not the greatest at growing food TREES though, so perhaps its just me. The pawpaw trees I planted remain barren, naked little sticks in the ground, as do the pluot trees. The avocado tree that was supposed to be cold hardy disintegrated. The satsuma tree that a driver from further south brought me gave up and died. No need to bring up the guava tree, ice cream banana tree or goji berry experiments. I should have known better. Stay in your ZONE Amylou! The pineberries grew but were gross. I do have some victories. The pink lemonade blueberry bush has done well. I bought it of course because it was a pink variety. I suppose it success was due to all the good pink vibes around it at my house. I got a dwarf mulberry that seems to be doing okay. No fruit yet but its alive! And one of the plum trees I planted a few years ago is thriving, though the fruit gets to be about as big as a dime before it starts to turn color and then fall off. I have NO idea what to do about that so whatever. The grape vines were doing great until the power company sent its goons out there (to the WRONG ADDRESS) to spray herbicide indiscriminately and killed them. Oafs. This year, I discovered the Black Beauty tomato. On first sight, it looked akin to those rainbow rose seeds you see scammers selling on eBay. Very unusual looking but attractive. But I did some research and then ordered a plant from a seller on etsy based in California. I also ordered a \"Blue Berries\" cherry tomato plant from the same seller, and will plant the two instead of the normal purple varieties I plant this year. A big step because my favorite cherry tomato is black cherry, and I am forgoing that this year to give these a chance. They arrive tomorrow. I am excited! I do hope though, that if they are going to fail, they do so immediately, so that I will be able to plant my purple regulars. But I hope they are a success! It's tedious, boring, my back and neck start to hurt, and many of the seeds I sow with a pair of tweezers.  I have trouble seeing close up when my contacts (for distance) are in, and if I'm wearing my glasses I have to take those off and on too.  Overall, it's just not really all that fun. My husband happened to walk by me yesterday as I was sowing and he says, you really like doing that, don't you?  And I said, No!  I really don't!  LOL. Perhaps if I had a dedicated work space - like a greenhouse or shed or garage space (all of which would be heated and comfy lol), that might help.  I do have to run outside and back in to get the potting mix, then carry the containers out into the (usually unpleasant) weather.  And if I had a dedicated work space I wouldn't have to worry so much about cleaning up the kitchen counter and sink after I sowed lol. Effects of Extreme Cold and Temperature Fluctuations Winter cold can be a double-edged sword for rose midges. Extended freezing temperatures dramatically reduce the survival of overwintering larvae/pupae in the soil pnwhandbooks.org. Extension entomologists note that \u201cvery low temperatures in winter significantly reduce overwintering populations\u201dpnwhandbooks.org of pests \u2013 rose midges included. In regions with harsh winters where the ground freezes deeply, a large portion of the cocoons near the surface may be killed by cold. For example, the Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks indicate that severe winter cold has a strong limiting effect on rose midge populationspnwhandbooks.org. Similarly, rose specialists often observe far fewer midges after an especially frigid winter, as many pupae cannot survive once soil temperatures drop well below freezing for prolonged periods. On the other hand, temperature fluctuations (freeze-thaw cycles) during winter can also influence survival. If an unseasonable warm spell in mid-winter causes soils to thaw and even reach near the development threshold, some pupae might prematurely resume development. A sudden return to freezing conditions can then be lethal to these dehardened or actively developing individuals. Even if the midges do not fully emerge, the loss of cold hardiness during a thaw can make them more vulnerable to subsequent freezes. Consistent with general overwintering biology, a stable cold dormancy is safer for insects than abrupt temperature swings. A deep snow cover or thick mulch layer can buffer these fluctuations by keeping soil temperature relatively steady (just around freezing) houzz.com \u2013 ironically insulating the pests as well as the plants. In fact, continuous snow cover in cold climates may allow more midges to survive by preventing the extreme cold from penetrating the soil and by avoiding repeated freeze-thaw cycles. Conversely, in open exposed soil, cycles of daytime thawing and night refreezing can increase mortality of the fragile cocoons.
